comment: Minimum PASSING test count per workspace, checked by scripts/check-test-floor.mjs. This is a RATCHET against a suite that silently shrinks, not a coverage target. It exists because `--experimental-test-isolation=none` (see .github/workflows/ci.yml) swallows a module-level throw once any test in that file has registered: the run goes green, exits 0, and simply reports fewer tests. Measured: 2174 instead of 2175, with `# fail 0`. A count floor is the only thing that turns that back into a red. Raise these when tests are added; lowering one is a deliberate act that should be explained in the commit. LOWERED 2026-08-19: backthread 729 -> 714 (712 after the removal, +3 for the retired-name tests: two behavioural, one over its source). The pre-edit PreToolUse hook was removed (founder decision, see cli/hooks/hooks.json's $comment_no_pretooluse_edit), retiring editNudge.test.ts's 15 tests and 2 `edit-context` dispatch tests in bin.test.ts. The suite shrank because the feature did, not because tests were dropped: the case that pinned the hook's existence was INVERTED into a guard in plugin.test.ts rather than deleted. RAISED 2026-08-21: backthread 715 -> 847 (+132), measured, for the failure-copy work. Nothing was removed: src/failureCopy.test.ts is new (the renderer, the endpoint registry, the guards, and a conformance battery of 4 properties x 9 rendered endpoints generated FROM the registry, so the count moves with the endpoint list), plus flag-dispatch cases in bin.test.ts and behavioural cases added to capture/infer/inflow/lesson/localDecisions/onboardingState tests. Several EXISTING tests changed their expected string rather than being dropped, because the rendered failure changed, which is the point of the change. The number rose across four rounds as three independent reviews each found real defects: two registry entries claiming a failure was never shown on surfaces that print it, the renderer treating `error` as always a machine slug when the worker also writes prose there, a bug-report tail appended to deliberate refusals, seven ways past the endpoint guard, and five surviving mutants. A fourth review then found a prototype-chain leak putting `function toString() { [native code] }` in front of a user, two copy entries advising the reader to ask owners of a repo that by definition has none, an instruction the MCP surface could not follow, six more ways past the endpoint guard, and nine survivors. A fifth review then found raw Postgres text still reaching a reader through the `error` field on Edge-Function 500s, four sentences wrong about the condition they fire on, three entries no reachable route sends, three more guard escapes, and thirteen survivors. The copy is now asserted SENTENCE BY SENTENCE rather than by length, because copy is the product here. A sixth review found the endpoint guard still passable by two ordinary spellings — an origin routed through a private helper, and one function that both built a URL and fetched it — while three shipped claims said it was not. Endpoints can now be born in exactly one module, that module is forbidden to make requests, and every export of it must be registered, and no request may be pointed at a URL that was invented or edited rather than built there. A seventh review found five more spellings past the previous version — surgery on a builder's result, a hardcoded host, a name-shaped exemption, an `export { }` list, and an origin interpolated in front of a path that the guard's own comment-stripper had erased before it looked. The stripper is a scanner now, because a regex pair ate from the `//` inside every URL string it was meant to find. Every one of those is a named test.  RAISED 2026-08-19: @backthread/extractor 2175 -> 2201 for packages/extractor/src/safety.test.ts — the source-tree budget and its symlink-escape guard, which previously had no test that failed when it broke. RAISED 2026-08-21: backthread 847 -> 865 (+18), measured, for the shell-command path harvest. Nothing was removed: the harvest that reads file paths out of Bash/shell command strings is new, and so is the gate that only emits a path the file actually exists in the working tree. An independent review then fuzzed it with 4,000 hostile commands and found real leaks the string rules could not catch -- a file reached after `cd` out of the repo, a scheme-less URL's hostname and route, string literals inside a heredoc, .git/ and node_modules/, a 16,892-character token and a command yielding 20,000 paths -- so the count also covers a named test per hostile input plus the two caps. Two claims the code did not honour were corrected rather than re-asserted: the extension list's longest-first sort was dead code (the trailing lookahead does that work) and the lookbehind was not what kept URLs out (the repo-root fence was). Tests now assert WHICH gate rejected a token, so a case cannot pass because a different rule happened to catch it.  RAISED 2026-08-29: backthread 865 -> 924 (+59), measured, for the containment-fence hardening. Nothing was removed. The additions are: six cases on the path fence itself (a caller-reported escape dropping a path from BOTH the tool-input and the shell route, the same caller reporting no escape leaving every path untouched, a dropped path not spending the shell budget, and a NUL byte refused from every origin); an end-to-end case built on real git repos, a real symlink out of the checkout and real files, which pins the two halves of the rule at once -- a path descending THROUGH a link into another repository is dropped, while this repo own name for a file that happens to be a link out is kept; and captureNotice.test.ts, which is new, covering the file capture leaves behind when it has something to say, because the shipped hook discards its own stdio and had no other channel. Two capture cases pin that the sentence reaches both stderr and that file, and one drives it end to end into the `backthread doctor` report. Three more came from an independent verification round: the cap boundary at 63/64/65 (a surviving mutant fired the notice at exactly the cap, announcing "the other 0"), and two end-to-end cases for a directory reached through a symlinked PARENT -- one a git checkout, one not a repo at all. The second is what makes resolving the root set load-bearing rather than defensive: with no git there the root set is the session cwd alone, carrying the symlinked spelling and no physical counterpart, so comparing a resolved path against the unresolved roots matches nothing and every path reads as having left a repo that does not exist. That mutant survived until this case existed. Five more came from an independent code review that found two live leaks the first round did not close. A sibling worktree could VOUCH for an escaping link: roots are checkouts of one repo, so every tracked directory exists in all of them, and a rule that kept a path as soon as some root resolved it inside let the sibling launder an escape at a name the repo genuinely has. And a link into a MISSING directory resolved nowhere, which read as an absence rather than a contradiction, so the same link leaked or did not purely by what sat on its far side. One case each, end to end on real repos and real links, plus the deleted-file property re-asserted inside the second so the ancestor climb cannot quietly take it away. Then prunable worktree registrations, which git still lists and which were spending capped verification slots and inflating the count reported to the reader -- two cases, one for the skip and one for the annotation not bleeding into the records after it. And isInsideRoot, which is exported with an injected separator ONLY so the win32 spelling can be exercised: realpath and join answer in the platform separator, a hardcoded slash makes every path below a root read as an escape there, and no test running on this machine can tell sep from a slash. That mutant survived an end-to-end test and dies against this one. Three more close claims that were written in comments and guarded by nothing, found by mutating them: the escape check being handed the roots the harvest ACTUALLY used rather than the caller list (it falls back to a root found in the transcript, and a predicate closed over the caller empty list can only ever answer no-escape), and the two doctor lines -- an absent notice must report the state of the mailbox and claim nothing about a capture that may never have happened, and a notice must warn with its date without ever driving the exit code.
